This lecture lays the groundwork for the third-year TMD course. Sometimes the occlusion has nothing to do with a patient's problem; other times, working on the occlusion helps the patient toward a good outcome even though it wasn't part of the cause. When a student asked whether every condition on the TMD classification list would be tested, he said to look for the general themes: the individual entities are the third-year course, and apart from one or two (such as local muscle soreness) he would not go into them in detail this year. Normal function and dysfunction The normal functions of the masticatory system are chewing, swallowing and speaking. Dysfunction is the alteration or inhibition of normal function. It usually shows up as an inability to move the way we should (can't chew, can't swallow), or as pain, which can be intense, severe and not easily treated. Dysfunction results from a functional disturbance: the functional disturbance is the cause, and often we don't know why it happened. Examples of dysfunction: muscle disorders (decreased range of motion; an acute malocclusion from a change in the resting length of the muscles); structural changes in the joint (deviations on opening or closure); occlusal overload associated with tooth fracture, pulpal pain, periodontal bone loss and tooth wear (most periodontal bone loss is from infection, but force plays a role); and headache. There are over 250 kinds of headache, and treating each may take something different. What a TMD is Patients say they "have TMJ," but the TMJ is the joint; the correct term is a temporomandibular disorder (TMD). A TMD is a collective term embracing a number of clinical problems that involve the masticatory muscles, the TMJ, or both. It is not one thing: it is a collection of different clinical entities (over 40), each different, and this has been one of the real problems in how dentistry has tried to treat "TMD patients." What they have in common is that most alter normal function and some, but not always, cause pain of varied severity. General types: problems in the muscles, maybe 50%; problems in the joints, maybe 35%; others (vascular, neurologic and more), and often combinations. The classification on the slides is Bell's, older but widely used, with four groups: masticatory muscle disorders; TMJ disorders (how the condyle and disc fit together, structural changes from development or trauma, and inflammatory disorders such as arthritis, retrodiscitis and synovitis); chronic mandibular hypomobility (ankylosis, contracture); and growth disorders. Every one of them is diagnosed and treated differently, so "I'm being treated for a TMD" tells you almost nothing. Myofascial pain, by contrast, is one specific TMD with its own features, such as trigger points. Many TMDs have nothing to do with occlusion, but all may be a functional disturbance. A TMD is not synonymous with orofacial pain, a much larger category of disorders of the head and neck that includes TMDs and other pains outside the masticatory structures. Pain also depends on how we interpret the world around us, so some of these problems are physical and some biopsychosocial. Dentistry has historically tied occlusion to TMD, which isn't a good thing to do, because occlusion doesn't relate to many of these entities. Why the tie? Things we do in the mouth often help. As he put it, "here's the way I'll say it in 2026": the occlusal work helps provide an environment of healing that helps resolve other disorders. Being a helpful adjunct does not make occlusion part of the cause. How a functional disturbance develops The model: Normal function + Event > Physiologic tolerance ⇒ Symptoms. Normal function. Chewing, swallowing and speaking are regulated by the brainstem (the central pattern generator and its engrams), influenced by peripheral sensory and nociceptive input (bite on something uncomfortable and a response happens) and by CNS effects such as the limbic system, which stress and behavior turn up or down. Events. Local events: a high crown or filling, tissue trauma (pizza that was too hot), muscle strain, blunt trauma or repeated microtrauma, bruxism, constant (deep) pain input; in fact any change in a sensory or proprioceptive input. Systemic events: emotions, stress, and feeling bad all over with the flu. Physiologic tolerance is the ability to tolerate an event, and it is affected by many factors. Local: the occlusion of the teeth defines a position of the mandible, which affects the joints, muscles, ligaments and orthopedic posture; an unstable orthopedic relationship of the mandible to the maxilla and cranial base. Systemic: genetics, gender, diet, acute or chronic disease. If normal function plus the event stays below the physiologic tolerance, the patient adapts and has no symptoms; most of the time we tolerate things fairly well. If it exceeds the tolerance, symptoms begin. Each element of the model can change, and an event tolerated on one day may not be tolerable on another. That is the story you hear from TMD patients again and again: fine all their life until last Monday, then on Tuesday intense pain, and you rarely know what changed. There is no sticker on anyone's forehead saying how much they will tolerate. When the tolerances of the masticatory system are exceeded, structures break down. The signs and symptoms: a. pulpitis (or hypersensitive teeth), b. tooth wear or fracture, c. tooth mobility, d. masticatory muscle pain, e. TMJ pain, f. ear pain, g. headache pain. The five etiologies of functional disturbances The list isn't complete, but these five are common: 1. mandibular stability, 2. trauma, 3. emotional stress, 4. deep pain input, 5. parafunctional activities. He spent the most time on mandibular stability, because that one is often directly in our hands. 1. Mandibular stability: what the evidence says Mandibular stability regards the simultaneous fit of the teeth and both joints against the skull. Research shows some relation of occlusion to functional disturbances, but the dental literature rarely says which TMD it studied, so its patient groups are mixed. "When I first learned this 35 years ago, it really hasn't changed a lot today." Pullinger and Seligman, a well-cited group of studies, noted a higher frequency of these signs in TMD patients: a skeletal anterior open bite, a CO to MIP slide greater than 2 mm, horizontal overjet greater than 4 mm (no good anterior guidance), and five or more missing posterior teeth. But the same signs are found in the non-TMD population, so the authors concluded that occlusion is not the most important factor in TMDs: multiple co-factors were more common. The textbook's review of 57 epidemiologic studies (Table 7-2): 22 found no relationship and 35 found occlusion related to TMD symptoms. The occlusal conditions varied widely from study to study, they don't always lead to symptoms, a relationship doesn't imply cause, and the studies usually don't specify the type of TMD. Overall, the evidence is lacking. Orthopedic stability and occlusal stability Despite the lack of evidence, it is widely accepted that sound occlusal relationships are the basis of successful dentistry: all teeth contact evenly and simultaneously; all contacts are between centric cusp tips and flattened surfaces, directing forces through the long axes; the anterior teeth disclude the posterior teeth (mutually protected occlusion). In patients with temporomandibular problems, following these same principles often helps. Ideally every part is stably seated: joints fully seated → orthopedic stability; teeth fully in contact (MIP) → occlusal stability. That leads to the treatment goals for the musculoskeletal stable position. For a muscle disorder, an inflammatory disorder or a severely debilitated dentition, provide optimum functional occlusion with the condyles in their most musculoskeletal stable position (centric relation): 1. The condyles rest in their most superior-anterior position against the slopes of the articular eminences. 2. The articular discs are properly interposed between the condyles and fossae (in some disc disorders this can't be achieved). 3. On closure in that position the posterior teeth contact evenly and simultaneously, centric cusp tips on flat surfaces, forces along the long axes. 4. In eccentric movement the anterior teeth contact and disclude the posterior teeth. 5. In the alert feeding position (head forward and down) the posterior contacts are more prominent than the anterior. Because these goals help treat functional disturbances, they also become the goals for permanently restoring the dentition. With the teeth apart, the muscles seat the joints: orthopedic stability. Keep the joints seated and close until the teeth touch, and in most people the result is occlusal instability: only about 10% have MIP coincident with closure in CR. Dental stability, prioritized for function, will sacrifice orthopedic stability: to bring the teeth into MIP, one or both joints come off their seat. Orthopedic instability: when the teeth are brought into MIP, one (or both) condyles are not in a stable relationship with the disc and fossa. A stable occlusion with unstable joints may lead to an intracapsular disorder (inside the joint capsule; one of the many TMDs, and a common one). Risk factors: the degree of discrepancy (a condylar misposition of 1-2 mm is not likely to create a problem; over 3 mm presents increased risk, and some would say 4 mm); and the amount of loading (patients who brux have greater risk). A greater risk does not mean the patient will have a problem. So in some circumstances occlusion can contribute to a functional disturbance. Dental malocclusion does influence function: a poor occlusion doesn't return the mandible to MIP as cleanly, and worn teeth change how we close. There are reports of more TMD with open bite or Angle Class II (a skeletal Class II patient tends to posture the jaw forward and has little anterior guidance), but they are not well supported by the literature. Malocclusion may only become important when considering joint position. His patient. When he was a resident, a woman came to the clinic in intense pain after seeing many dentists. She had a lot of crown and bridge work and had been fine until, one day, she wasn't. His program director, who listened and understood what was going on, put her in a full-coverage splint, adjusted over months so that all the teeth touched. As the splint let her condyles return to a seated position, an open bite appeared: years of restorations had built her teeth to MIP while moving her farther and farther from orthopedic stability, to keep dental stability. She was held at the new position with the splint, restored in provisionals at that vertical for well over a year, then moved to her final restorations, about two years in all. Was occlusion an issue here? Definitely yes. That is how orthopedic instability can lead to a problem, but in many other TMDs it isn't the case. Occlusal instability and muscle function Example 1: unexpected contact. Bite unexpectedly on something hard and you reflexively open: a protective nociceptive reflex, rapid, involuntary and subconscious, in the trigeminal motor nucleus. It is a complex reflex, because opening means shutting down many muscles and activating many others. Example 2: stimulating the masticatory muscles. From EMG studies: if mediotrusive contacts are eliminated, the masseter and temporalis are not activated by a mediotrusive movement. This supports canine guidance. In the classic study (Manns, 1989), a full-coverage maxillary splint was divided into anterior, premolar (intermediate) and molar (posterior) blocks and the EMG recorded with each. Without posterior contact, muscle activity dropped significantly; adding the molar contacts brought it up to full. Two theories came out of it: 1. anterior tooth contact inhibits muscle contraction; 2. a lack of posterior tooth contact fails to activate muscle contraction. Later studies confirmed the second. Posterior contact stimulates the elevator muscles: bite, crunch, close down. That is how we're wired. The masticatory muscles have two basic activities. Ortho-function (normal function): elevation, depression, laterotrusion and so on; protective reflexes are present; tooth contacts affect specific muscle groups, and posterior contact stimulates the elevators. Parafunction: clenching, grinding (bruxism) and oral habits. "All bets are off": muscles fire without that feedback from the mouth, agonists and antagonists fight each other, and the hyperactivity raises muscle tonus, giving fatigue and strain. These are very different mechanisms, and they are not influenced by tooth contacts as was once thought. The "high" crown. You deliver a crown on #19 that is slightly high (the jaw can feel microns). The patient develops protective muscle co-contraction, a TMD of muscle origin: restricted or guarded mandibular movement from co-contraction of the muscles, as a way to avoid pain from the initial event. There is "nothing pathologic about it": it is a normal, healthy avoidance behavior, and the source can be a high crown, a tooth with an endodontic lesion or a burned palate. But moving in ways we don't normally move leads to generalized muscle soreness and pain (local muscle soreness, myalgia). The conclusion: an unstable occlusal contact influenced muscle activity. Does occlusion cause a specific TMD? In this case, yes. Existing interferences are another matter. Posterior mediotrusive (non-working) and laterotrusive (working) contacts are equally noted in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients: "that's a very important point." A CO-MIP slide under 2 mm has equal incidence in both groups; over 2 mm, the incidence increases in symptomatic patients; interferences to maximum closure are more common in symptomatic patients. Incidence does not prove causality. Summary. Altering an occlusal contact does influence muscle activity. Introducing an interference can lead to pain or dysfunction. Eliminating existing interferences does not seem to significantly alter the symptoms of TMD. Limited data suggest an interference-free occlusion is associated with a lower incidence of TMD symptoms developing. Current practice: equilibrating a patient's occlusion for prevention is not supported. So when you deliver a crown or a filling, avoid putting in a mediotrusive contact, because that's too sudden a change; but if the patient already had one, taking it away is probably not going to change their symptoms. The precise effect of occlusal stability on symptoms hasn't been established: sometimes related, sometimes not. A better question: does CNS posturing of the mandible anteriorly or anterolaterally to MIP increase risk as a co-factor for muscle and joint disorders? To sum up occlusion and functional disturbances: acute changes produce protective co-contraction, but most often new engrams develop with little consequence once the interference is resolved. Orthopedic instability must be considerable to matter, and it needs loading forces (such as parafunction) to destabilize. Occlusal problems that weren't a problem before may become one if an event finally exceeds the tolerance, or the tolerance changes: "the straw that broke the camel's back." Two general statements, explored in the TMD course, with exceptions: problems bringing the teeth together (mandibular movement) are often manifested in the muscles; once the teeth are in occlusion, problems with applying force are often manifested in the joints. Occlusal therapy to establish stability Occlusal therapy is a general term for any treatment that alters a patient's occlusal condition. It can be reversible (non-invasive or temporary) or irreversible (invasive or permanent). Occlusal therapies are used for many dental needs (caries, esthetics); here the subject is the smaller group of patients with a functional disturbance, where you think changing the occlusion matters. Patient education Occlusal equilibration Physical therapy (self or professional assist) Restorative dentistry Pharmacotherapy Repositioning splint Counseling Orthodontics Flat plane stabilization splint (the one that changes occlusal stability) Orthognathic surgery, arthroscopy, open joint surgery Splint therapy treats muscle pain, protects teeth and restorations (for example in bruxism), alleviates joint pain (less force into the joint) and is part of trial therapy. The splint is a plastic covering over the occlusal surfaces with a new occlusal surface built on it: whatever MIP was, it's gone. The goal of a stabilization splint is to have the joints seated and new contacts against the plastic. It is "hugely effective," so effective it led dentistry to conclude occlusion must be the problem. Not the case. Splints can be maxillary or mandibular, full or partial arch, and stabilizing or repositioning. A stabilizing splint provides occlusal (dental) stability while the joints are seated in an orthopedically stable relationship. A repositioning splint is used in disc displacements, sleep apnea and other cases where a specific non-centric mandibular position is wanted. Many names: occlusal splints, devices or appliances, night guards, anterior bite plates, posterior pivots. Both maxillary and mandibular splints can provide a perfect dental occlusion coinciding with orthopedic stability. A maxillary splint has a posterior flat plane (no indentations or elevations, so no eccentric contacts) with an anterior ramp; it is very stable and retentive, sturdier and less likely to fracture (better for heavy clenchers), easier to get anterior contacts on and to adjust, usable in Class I, II and even III, and ideally suited for Class II division 1 (excessive horizontal overlap). It is visible, so normally for nighttime. A mandibular splint (its ramp behind the front teeth) causes less speech interference and is less visible when speaking, so it is preferable for daytime wear; he makes many for athletes. Full coverage covers all the teeth in the arch, reduces the chance of teeth moving and is recommended in almost all situations: by far the most effective splint, and patients in pain want to keep it in. Partial coverage may let covered teeth intrude and uncovered teeth extrude (supereruption), may not be as effective, and small ones can be an aspiration hazard at night; whether they are easier to wear is questionable. Irreversible treatment. Without a functional disturbance, irreversible treatment for broken, decayed or missing teeth is simply the bulk of the dental care dentists provide. If a functional disturbance is present, irreversible occlusal treatment is only indicated when sufficient evidence suggests the primary etiologic factor is the mandibular instability (the occlusal condition): you can't ungrind a tooth. In general, perform the least amount of dental alteration that fulfills the treatment goal, and choose the type of therapy by the severity of the malocclusion. Selective grinding (equilibration, occlusal adjustment) is minor reshaping of enamel surfaces; avoid exposing dentin and creating iatrogenic sensitivity (if it would reach dentin, restore instead). Technique: 1. eliminate prematurities (contacts on initial closure), 2. eliminate interferences (contacts blocking a movement), 3. direct centric forces axially, 4. establish optimum occlusion (details in the textbook). When the interarch alignment deviates farther from ideal, grinding would expose dentin or mutilate the teeth, so use fixed prosthetics and minor orthodontics (properly done, Invisalign can act as splint and tooth movement at once). Major deviations from ideal interarch relations need orthodontics, orthognathic surgery and prosthetics. The rule of thirds simplifies the choice: mark the contacts with the condyles in the desired position; if the discrepancy falls in the first third of the tooth, selective grinding; the middle third, minor orthodontics and fixed prosthetics (most deviations are here); beyond that, major orthodontics, orthognathic surgery and prosthetics. Success. The evidence is weak: a lack of scientific evidence relating therapy to effects (the standard is the double-blind clinical trial), a lack of agreement on TMD diagnostic categories, and some causal factors are hard to control (emotional stress). Long-term success of reversible and irreversible treatments is similar, 50-90%. So the treatment philosophy: because conservative treatment reports similar success, it is the first attempt; non-conservative treatment is attempted if conservative approaches fail. Other factors in the choice: symptoms, condition of the dentition, systemic health, esthetics and finances. A splint is cheap and easy, but a patient can't chew and eat with it all their life. Consider the population in four groups: no dental treatment needed and TMD asymptomatic (the basic hygiene patient); dental treatment needed, TMD asymptomatic (the bulk of patients, "where we make our living"); TMD symptomatic, no dental treatment needed; and the "red light" group: TMD symptomatic and needing a lot of dental treatment, where guidance is hardest. 2. Trauma "A force is only traumatic when it produces trauma." What makes a force (occlusal, external) traumatic is characterized by five factors: 1. magnitude (how great), 2. frequency (how often), 3. duration (how long it acts), 4. direction (we handle vertical forces well, horizontal forces poorly), 5. distribution (how many teeth resist it; for example posterior bite collapse). Combined, these may lead to dysfunction. Types of trauma: macrotrauma, a sudden force resulting in structural alterations (auto accidents, acceleration-deceleration injuries); microtrauma, small repetitive forces over time (for example bruxism). Common outcomes: orthopedic trauma (a broken jaw), intracapsular disorders (a blow to the side of the face), and direct damage to the teeth and alveolus: cracks and fractures, mobility, and wear. Occlusal trauma may produce histologic changes: injury to the PDL, bone resorption, cemental changes, vascular injury, pulpal hyperemia (questioned). Clinical findings: tooth mobility, tooth migration, attrition, widening of the PDL, tenderness to pressure, pulpal pain, and flattening of the TM joint (controversial). Where: the attachment apparatus (the PDL and adjacent structures) is the usual site; the gingiva and mucosa rarely. Recall that the stability of the connective tissue attachment, affected by inflammatory and not occlusal factors, determines whether bone loss may be reversible. Tooth mobility Vertical mobility is related to the root's surface area and shape. A healthy tooth shows no clinically observable vertical mobility, but the actual initial vertical movement is about 28 µm, the same for anterior and posterior teeth. The immediate rebound is about 7 µm, and full recovery takes almost 4 hours. An implant moves only 2-3 µm under a 10-lb force, from the viscoelastic strain of the bony interface: the reason implant occlusion is handled differently. Horizontal mobility is always greater than vertical. Single-rooted teeth are more mobile than multi-rooted, and the amount depends on the width of the PDL, the root attachment area, the elasticity of the alveolus and the function (position) of the tooth. A force of about 500 g moves a tooth horizontally 56 to 108 µm; 150 µm is the limit of physiologic horizontal mobility, and beyond it mobility is abnormal or pathologic, an outcome of a functional disturbance. Mobility changes through the day: greatest on arising from sleep, least late in the day after function. Adapted mobility: the tissues adapt or cope and the changes are not progressive; the increased mobility is self-limiting, and a tooth may stay that way for years. Traumatic mobility: the adaptive capacity (biological tolerance) is exceeded, and the mobility increases progressively; this is an indication for splinting the teeth (more surface area to resist the force). To tell them apart you must monitor over time: increasing mobility needs treatment; stable mobility is less of an indication. Miller's Mobility Index (1938): the tooth is held firmly between two instruments and moved back and forth. 0, no detectable movement; 1, barely distinguishable movement; 2, any horizontal movement up to 1 mm; 3, more than 1 mm, or depressed or rotated (vertical movement). The scale has been modified many times. Dental wear Wear dates from recent to prehistoric times, when an abrasive diet (food ground with stones) was the usual cause. Physiologic wear is wear acceptable for the patient's age (a 75-year-old has chewed for 60 years); the same wear at 30 is not. Pain is usually not a symptom: wear is too slow. Patients usually seek treatment for esthetics, and by then an easy treatment is usually too late. If wear is pathologic, treatment is indicated; it won't get better on its own. Treatment: best before the wear extends to multiple teeth (twenty worn teeth at about $1,200 a crown is very expensive). The canines and incisors involved in anterior guidance are often the first to wear (early signs); without guidance, posterior wear can be significant because forces increase toward the back. Severe wear may need crown lengthening, endodontics or orthodontic extrusion before prosthodontics. General rule: if 3 mm of tooth structure is coronal to the papilla, crown lengthening is often not indicated. Attrition Tooth-to-tooth grinding from normal or parafunctional activity (often bruxism) Facets match and are only at occlusal contacts; shiny with sharp edges; enamel and dentin in the facet at the same height Abrasion "Third-body wear": mechanical raking of a foreign material; habitual Food particles, chewing tobacco; most common is toothbrush-assisted wear Erosion "Chemically assisted wear": acid dissolution, intrinsic (gastric acid) or extrinsic (food and drink acid) Extends beyond the occlusal contacts; dull facets; cupping (dentin wears faster than enamel); "proud restorations" standing above the eroded tooth Abfraction Loss of tooth structure from flexural biomechanical loading (Latin, "to break away") A notch near the CEJ, usually facial; saliva may add "stress corrosion" Wear mechanisms frequently act together, and the presence of acid accelerates mechanical wear. (In class he said that with erosion alone the facets don't match each other, because it isn't a tooth-to-tooth contact.) Many extrinsic acids also carry sucrose, adding a caries problem. Erosion patterns. GERD: the classic appearance is erosion on the lingual of all the maxillary teeth to the second molars and the occlusal surfaces of the mandibular molars; often asymmetrical, because in sleep the refluxed acid rolls off the tongue onto the lingual surfaces and patients have a preferred side to sleep on (on the back, both sides). Bulimia nervosa (recurrent binge eating followed by purging, fasting, laxatives, enemas, diuretics or over-exercising): erosion mostly on the maxillary anterior teeth, sometimes to the first premolar, posterior teeth only when long-standing; the maxillary anteriors can be completely destroyed while the mandibular anteriors are not (protected by the tongue and saliva). Carbonated beverage abuse: pattern 1, swish and hold in the vestibule to fizz, then swallow, giving generalized erosion with a satin appearance and islands of exposed dentin; pattern 2, pooling the drink in the back of the mouth to fizz and cool, very severe, with high caries and more wear on the back and front teeth. Citrus fruit abuse: type 1, biting fruit and sucking the juice through the teeth, erodes the front teeth to a "screwdriver" appearance; type 2, biting and chewing on the molars, looks like beverage pooling, with more posterior wear. Less common: drug abuse (aspirin, meth), swimming (chlorinated water, on the side they breathe on) and occupational exposure (battery and galvanizing workers). Noncarious cervical lesions (NCCLs) are one of the most common demineralization diseases in the body: a cervical defect either smooth, rounded and saucer-like (growing more in height) or a sharp V-shaped notch (growing in height and depth). Caries is often not present but can develop (arrest it with silver diamine fluoride). Prevalence varies in the literature from 10% to 90%, but all accept it increases with age. They are found throughout the mouth, most often on the facial surfaces of maxillary premolars; lingual lesions occur but are rarely severe. Treatment with resin composite is typically delayed until necessary: progression, sensitivity or quality of life, poor esthetics, food collection. The etiology is multifactorial: excessive horizontal toothbrushing, acidic foods and drinks, reflux disease; occlusal factors are associated but not sufficient alone. The concept of abfraction (tensile fatigue flexing the cervical area under occlusal load, separating enamel rods, with saliva inducing "stress corrosion") is supported by in vitro studies, but clinical documentation has neither validated nor rejected it, so it isn't included as a primary mechanism of wear. Clenching, nail biting and a diagnosis of TMD are significantly associated with NCCLs, and the sustained loads of clenching and nail biting are more damaging to mineralized tissue than the dynamic, shifting loads of bruxism. 3. Emotional stress and 4. deep pain input Emotional stress. The emotional centers influence muscle function through the hypothalamus, the reticular system and the limbic system. For example, gamma efferents stimulate the intrafusal fibers of the muscle spindles to contract, "sensitizing" the muscle and raising its tonicity, often in the head and neck. (The muscle spindle is the major sensory organ of muscle: intrafusal fibers, innervated by gamma efferents, lie parallel to the extrafusal fibers and sense the change in muscle length and velocity.) In that state almost anything, such as an unexpected passive stretch, is perceived as pain. That's the physiologic reason you feel tight and worn out after three weeks of studying for an occlusion test. Deep pain input (deep is anything below the skin or mucosa; superficial is on it) is often overlooked. Example: limited opening with odontogenic pain; resolve the pulpal problem (an extraction, say) and the opening returns to normal. Remote pain, such as cervical pain, may affect the masticatory system, and referred pain is covered next year. We don't chew, speak and swallow the same way when we hurt. Nociception also inhibits motor output (a guarded protection of damaged tissue), so altered pathways must be activated to keep functioning. 5. Parafunctional activities Parafunctional activities are movements outside normal function. They can lead to a functional disturbance, and because they are subconscious they are difficult to manage. Daytime (diurnal): clenching (often tied to stress; these patients often have a history of fractured, chipped, broken or splayed teeth, and tori or exostoses are common); grinding (by different mechanisms than at night); oral habits (cheek and tongue biting, finger and thumb sucking); unusual postural habits; occupational habits (biting pencils, pens or nails; holding a telephone or violin under the chin). Nighttime (nocturnal): bruxism, rhythmic contractions causing clenching and grinding during sleep; tongue compression (can move teeth, and leaves a scalloped lateral border of the tongue); cheek biting. Bruxism is very damaging. Compared with function (Table 7-3, Okeson), its forces are often three to five times greater, they are horizontal rather than down the long axis, the mandible can be in any position (eventually MIP itself is worn away), the muscles work differently, and the protective reflexes are absent because we are asleep. Sleep phases come from EEG monitoring: about 80% non-REM (physical rest) and 20% REM (psychic rest). Bruxism is associated with a change from a deeper to a lighter phase of sleep (arousal phases); in research, flashing lights, sound or touch can induce a grinding event. Duration varies: most bruxers have many short events of 5-10 seconds (the slides total 12-40 minutes a night), and patients vary in how much damage they show. Causes of bruxism. Bruxism is centrally mediated (CNS): probably more related to something like restless leg syndrome than to the occlusion. Besides the changes in sleep phase, there is a relationship to oxygen saturation (an association with sleep apnea). It is influenced by emotional stress, medications and genetic predisposition. Occlusion? Recent studies do not support that occlusal contact initiates bruxism events as was once thought. The primary treatment is a stabilization splint. Placing it gives a temporary cessation of bruxism (a temporary muscle discoordination; in class he said a couple of days to a couple of weeks, the slides say weeks to months), and then the bruxism returns, because it is centrally mediated. So the goal is to brux against the splint and preserve the teeth: "brux against the $400 splint and avoid the $40,000 rehab." There is no cure. Additional recommendations, with little supporting evidence: sleeping on the side, stress management, avoiding alcohol, smoking cessation, hypnosis, acupuncture. Stress and muscle activity. Rugh's data tracked nighttime masseter EMG over days against life events: activity rose with a job interview, a fight with a parent or quitting a job, and fell on a vacation in Hawaii; stress, pain and nocturnal muscle activity were well correlated. Patients bring baggage you often don't know about, which is why the TMD course stresses a multidisciplinary approach: other health care providers help with things a dentist can't. Bruxism in children is common (it can sound like a thousand violins) and is not considered to be associated with symptoms. It seems related to the developing dentition looking for occlusal stability, a different mechanism. Tell concerned parents it is often benign and to monitor; if masticatory function is affected, the child should be evaluated by a dentist. Most of those teeth are primary teeth and will be lost. His close: occlusion matters significantly in a few of these disorders, but the vast majority have nothing to do with it. Yet for most of them a simple stabilization splint provides an environment of healing that helps resolve the symptoms. It is not treating the etiology, and it doesn't mean occlusion was the cause.
